title: Evidence before the Southborough (Franchise) Committee
occasion: Oral examination by the Reforms Committee (Franchise) planning the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms.
summary: The 27-year-old professor explained to a British committee that "touchable" and "untouchable" Hindus were separate social groups and asked for separate representation for the untouchables.
keyIdea: People who are kept apart socially need their own representatives to be heard.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 1, p. 243–278

place: Bhima Koregaon war memorial, near Poona
title: Great Fight
occasion: New Year meeting of the Depressed Classes at the Koregaon War Memorial.
summary: He told the audience that hundreds of fighters from their community had fought on the British side, yet the British later called them a non-military community, and that caste Hindus still treated them as untouchables.
keyIdea: The community's record of courage disproves the label of inferiority.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 3–7

title: On Budget (maiden speech)
occasion: Budget debate, a week after he was sworn in as a nominated member (18 February 1927).
summary: His first speech in a legislature criticised a tax system that hit poor farmers hardest and argued for spending on education, health and prohibition.
keyIdea: A state that beggars its people ends by beggaring itself; progress has to be paid for.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 1–5

title: Mahad (Kolaba District Depressed Classes) Conference and march to the Chavdar Tank
occasion: Two-day conference after which the delegates walked to the public Chavdar Tank and drank its water (20 March 1927).
summary: At this conference Ambedkar asked the depressed classes to give up eating carrion and to root out ideas of high and low among themselves; the march to the tank that followed began the Mahad Satyagraha.
keyIdea: Using a public water source is a basic human right, not a favour.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 1, p. 3–20

title: Address at the Mahad Satyagraha Conference
occasion: Satyagraha Conference, during which the Manu Smriti was publicly burnt.
summary: BAWS prints a summary of his presidential address. He compared the conference to the French National Assembly of 1789 and said the movement aimed to remove social inequality, not just to win access to water; the Manu Smriti was burnt the same day.
keyIdea: The fight is for equality and human dignity, not only for water.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 1, p. 21–30

title: On the Maternity Benefit Bill
occasion: First reading of a bill to give maternity benefit to women factory workers.
summary: He supported paid maternity leave and argued that the government should share the cost because the nation benefits from healthy mothers and children.
keyIdea: Protecting working mothers is a duty of the whole society.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 166–167

title: Evidence before the Indian Statutory (Simon) Commission
occasion: Oral evidence on behalf of the Bahishkrita Hitakarini Sabha.
summary: Questioned on the two memoranda of the Bahishkrita Hitakarini Sabha, he argued for special representation and adult suffrage for the depressed classes.
keyIdea: The depressed classes must be treated as a distinct minority with political safeguards.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 459–490

title: We Are a Warrior Clan
occasion: Second session of the Ratnagiri District Bahishkrit Parishad.
summary: He told the conference that they must abolish their slavery themselves and that it was disgraceful to live at the cost of one's self-respect.
keyIdea: Without self-respect a person is a mere cipher.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 10–11

title: Speech at the Kalaram Temple Entry Satyagraha conference
occasion: Conference held on the eve of the satyagraha to enter the Kalaram temple, which began on 3 March 1930.
summary: BAWS reprints the account of the conference, at which Ambedkar launched the temple-entry satyagraha at Nasik.
keyIdea: The untouchables must assert their equal right to enter public temples.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 1, p. 181–190

title: Presidential address, All-India Depressed Classes Congress
occasion: First session of the All-India Depressed Classes Congress, before the first Round Table Conference.
summary: He supported self-government for India but warned that unless social realities were recognised, political power would pass into the hands of the upper castes.
keyIdea: Freedom for India must include political power for the depressed classes.

source.label: BAWS Vol. 17 Part 3 – Presidential Address, All India Depressed Classes Congress, Nagpur, 8 Aug 1930 (address begins at this page)

title: Speech at the Plenary Session, first Round Table Conference
occasion: Fifth sitting of the plenary session.
summary: Speaking for the depressed classes, he said British rule had not removed their grievances and that they also wanted a responsible government in which they had a share of power.
keyIdea: Nobody can remove our grievances as well as we can, and we need political power to do it.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 503–509

title: In Sub-Committee No. III (Minorities), first Round Table Conference
occasion: Second sitting of the Minorities Sub-Committee.
summary: He set out the conditions on which the depressed classes would accept majority rule in a self-governing India.
keyIdea: Minorities need written guarantees in the constitution.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 528–533

title: I Have No Homeland (meeting with Gandhi)
occasion: First meeting with Gandhi before the second Round Table Conference.
summary: In this conversation, reconstructed in BAWS from Marathi sources, Ambedkar told Gandhi that he had no homeland: he asked how he could call a land his own where his people were treated worse than cats and dogs and could not get water to drink.
keyIdea: Patriotism means little to people denied basic human dignity.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 1, p. 51–56

title: In the Federal Structure Committee, second Round Table Conference
occasion: Speeches in the Federal Structure Committee, 16 September – 16 November 1931.
summary: He discussed the shape of an Indian federation, the princely states and the powers of the centre.
keyIdea: A federation must be built on responsible, democratic government.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 600–651

title: In the Minorities Committee, second Round Table Conference
occasion: Seventh to ninth sittings of the Minorities Committee (28 September – 8 October 1931).
summary: He pressed the depressed classes' claim to special representation; in the same committee Gandhi declared that he would oppose separate electorates for the untouchables.
keyIdea: The depressed classes must be recognised as a separate minority.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 652–663

title: Questions to Winston Churchill before the Joint Committee on Indian Constitutional Reform
occasion: Examination of witnesses by the Joint Select Committee of the British Parliament.
summary: Ambedkar questioned Churchill and other witnesses about the safeguards in the proposed constitution.
keyIdea: Indian voices must be heard on India's constitution.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 742–745

title: Unfortunately I Was Born a Hindu Untouchable, but I Will Not Die a Hindu
occasion: Conference of the Depressed Classes of the Bombay Presidency.
summary: After ten years of struggle for equal treatment within Hinduism, he announced that he would leave the Hindu religion. BAWS gives a reported account (from Keer's biography), not a full verbatim text.
keyIdea: He was born a Hindu untouchable but would not die a Hindu (the conference title in BAWS).

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 94–99

title: What Path to Salvation? (Mukti Kon Pathe)
occasion: Bombay Presidency Mahar Conference, 30–31 May 1936.
summary: A long speech in Marathi explaining why conversion was needed for both material and spiritual reasons, and why the untouchables would never get equality inside Hinduism.
keyIdea: Religion is for man, not man for religion.

source.label: Columbia University (Frances Pritchett) – English translation by Vasant W. Moon

title: On a Bill to Abolish the Khoti System
occasion: Introduction of his private bill.
summary: He explained how the khoti landlord system in the Konkan exploited tenant farmers and asked the House to abolish it.
keyIdea: Land tenure should not make farmers into serfs.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 101–103

title: Trade Unions Must Enter Politics to Protect Their Interests
occasion: Conference of untouchable workers of the G.I.P. Railway, 12–13 February 1938.
summary: He told the workers that their two enemies were Brahmanism and capitalism, and that trade unions had to take part in politics.
keyIdea: Workers must organise politically, not only economically.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 173–192

title: On the Industrial Disputes Bill
occasion: First reading of the Bombay Industrial Disputes Bill.
summary: He opposed the bill because it penalised strikes, arguing that to punish a strike is to force a man to serve against his will.
keyIdea: To penalise a strike is nothing short of making the worker a slave.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 201–232

place: Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics, Poona
title: Federation versus Freedom (Kale Memorial Lecture)
occasion: Annual function of the Gokhale Institute.
summary: A long lecture analysing the federal scheme of the Government of India Act, 1935, which he argued would not bring real freedom.
keyIdea: A badly designed federation can block freedom instead of advancing it.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 1, p. 279–354

title: On Participation in the War
occasion: Debate on the Congress ministry's resolution about India's involvement in the Second World War (25–27 October 1939).
summary: He spoke on the war resolution and asked the House to consider what position the untouchables would have in a future Indian democracy, living in separate quarters on the edge of every village.
keyIdea: Indian self-government must include protections for minorities.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 2, p. 238–262

title: Why Indian Labour Is Determined to Win the War
occasion: Radio broadcast as Labour Member (printed in "Indian Information", 1 January 1943).
summary: He explained why workers should back the war against Nazism and said the war must bring a new order of liberty, equality and fraternity.
keyIdea: Victory must bring a new social order, not a return to the old one.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 10, p. 36–43

title: If Democracy Dies It Will Be Our Doom
occasion: All-India Depressed Classes Conference, third session, 18–20 July 1942, at which the All India Scheduled Castes Federation was founded.
summary: BAWS reprints the report of the conference, which drew huge crowds (over fifty thousand people met him at the railway station, according to the report), and his address on why the depressed classes must defend democracy.
keyIdea: The depressed classes must defend democracy, because its death would be their doom.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 242–272

title: Educate, Agitate, Organize; Have Faith and Lose No Hope
occasion: Reply to the address presented by the Reception Committee of the Depressed Classes Conference.
summary: He summed up his message to his followers in a three-part motto and urged them not to lose hope.
keyIdea: Educate, agitate, organise (the title of this speech in BAWS).

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 273–276

title: Progress of the Community Is Measured by Progress of Women
occasion: Second session of the All-India Depressed Classes Women's Conference.
summary: Speaking to a crowd that included some 20,000–25,000 women, he told them to keep clean, educate their children, remove their sense of inferiority and not hurry into marriage.
keyIdea: He measured the progress of a community by the progress its women had made.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 277–283

title: Ranade, Gandhi and Jinnah
occasion: 101st birth anniversary of Mahadev Govind Ranade, organised by the Deccan Sabha.
summary: He honoured Ranade as a social reformer and criticised blind hero-worship in Indian politics.
keyIdea: Hero-worship is dangerous for democracy.

source.label: Columbia University (Frances Pritchett) – full text from the 1943 edition

title: Labour and Parliamentary Democracy
occasion: Concluding session of the All-India Trade Union Workers' Study Camp (8–17 September 1943).
summary: He told trade unionists what real democracy should mean for workers and why labour needed its own political party.
keyIdea: Democracy must deliver social and economic justice, not just elections.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 10, p. 106–112

title: Indian History Is Nothing but a Struggle between Buddhism and Brahminism ("Rationalism in India")
occasion: Lecture arranged by the Madras Rational Society.
summary: He described Indian history as a long conflict between Buddhism and Brahmanism.
keyIdea: Indian history is a struggle between Buddhism and Brahmanism (title in BAWS).

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 334–336

title: Newspaper in a Modern Democratic System Is the Fundamental Basis of Good Government
occasion: Inauguration of the "People's Herald", weekly organ of the All-India Scheduled Castes Federation.
summary: He spoke about the role of newspapers in a democracy and about the future of the Indian National Congress.
keyIdea: Without its own press, a community cannot be heard.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 346–350

title: Communal Deadlock and a Way to Solve It
occasion: Session of the All India Scheduled Castes Federation.
summary: He proposed a way of sharing seats among communities in which no single community would have an absolute majority.
keyIdea: Majority rule by one community is untenable; a majority may have a relative majority only.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 1, p. 355–380

title: Speech on the Objectives Resolution
occasion: Debate on Jawaharlal Nehru's "Aims and Objects" resolution.
summary: He supported the ideals of the resolution but urged the Assembly to wait for the Muslim League and the princely states, and declared his faith that India would one day be united.
keyIdea: Given time and circumstances, nothing would prevent India from becoming one.

source.label: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. 1, 17 December 1946 (constitutionofindia.net)

audioOrVideo.note: Archival recording of his voice credited to Prasar Bharati Archives, published with photos and subtitles by the official MyGov India channel (11:39).

title: The Minority Must Always Be Won Over; It Must Never Be Dictated To
occasion: Inauguration of the Siddharth College Parliament.
summary: He spoke to students about the political losses suffered by the Scheduled Castes and about how majorities should treat minorities.
keyIdea: A majority must win over a minority, not dictate to it.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 374–383

title: Organise under One Leader, One Party, One Programme
occasion: Fifth United Provinces Scheduled Castes Federation conference, 24–25 April 1948.
summary: He urged the Scheduled Castes to unite politically under one organisation.
keyIdea: Political unity is the source of strength.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 388–394

title: Introducing the Draft Constitution
occasion: Motion to take the Draft Constitution into consideration.
summary: He explained the main features of the Draft Constitution, defended its choices (such as a strong centre and detailed provisions) and spoke of the need for "constitutional morality".
keyIdea: Democracy needs constitutional morality to be cultivated among the people.

source.label: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. 7, 4 November 1948 (constitutionofindia.net)

title: On Draft Article 25 (Right to Constitutional Remedies, now Article 32)
occasion: Clause-by-clause debate on the Draft Constitution.
summary: He called the article giving citizens the right to go to the Supreme Court to protect their fundamental rights the most important in the Constitution.
keyIdea: He described this article as "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it".

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 13, p. 434–443

title: Final speech before the adoption of the Constitution
occasion: Third reading of the Constitution.
summary: He reviewed the work of the Assembly and gave three warnings: use constitutional methods rather than the "grammar of anarchy", do not lay liberties at the feet of a great man, and turn political democracy into social democracy.
keyIdea: Political democracy cannot last unless there is social democracy, recognising liberty, equality and fraternity.

source.label: Constituent Assembly Debates, 25 November 1949 (constitutionofindia.net; BAWS cites CAD Vol. X, the website files it under Vol. 11)

title: Non-Believers Should Be Converted to the Eight-Fold Path
occasion: Conference of the World Fellowship of Buddhists, attended by representatives of 27 countries (BAWS).
summary: He spoke to the Buddhist delegates about spreading the Buddha's teaching.
keyIdea: Buddhism should actively spread its message (title in BAWS).

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 404–405

title: Buddhism Paved Way for Democracy and Socialistic Pattern of Society
occasion: Conference of the World Fellowship of Buddhists (25 May – 6 June 1950).
summary: He told an international Buddhist gathering that he wanted to understand why Buddhism rose so high and then disappeared in India, and spoke of its democratic spirit.
keyIdea: Buddhism carries the values of democracy and equality.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 406–409

title: The Bill Was Aimed at the Social Advancement of Women
occasion: Rally of about 50,000 people organised by the Belgaum District branch of the Scheduled Castes Federation (as reported in BAWS).
summary: He explained that the Hindu Code Bill was meant to improve the social position of women.
keyIdea: Law reform should give women equal rights in the family.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 411

title: Statement in explanation of his resignation from the Cabinet
occasion: Resignation as Law Minister; he was not allowed to read the statement in the House and released it to the press.
summary: He listed his reasons for leaving: the fate of the Hindu Code Bill, neglect of the Scheduled Castes, disagreement on foreign policy and Kashmir, and the way the Cabinet worked.
keyIdea: He would not stay in a government that let the Hindu Code Bill die.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 14 Part 2, p. 1315–1327

title: Failure of Parliamentary Democracy Will Result in Rebellion, Anarchy and Communism
occasion: Address to the students' parliament during the 1951–52 election campaign.
summary: He explained how parliamentary democracy works and warned of what would happen if it failed to deliver social and economic justice.
keyIdea: Parliamentary democracy must solve real problems or people will turn away from it.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 422–428

title: Conditions Precedent for the Successful Working of Democracy
occasion: Unveiling of a portrait and opening of a book collection at the Poona District Law Library.
summary: He listed the conditions democracy needs: no glaring inequalities, a real opposition, equality in law and administration, constitutional morality, no tyranny of the majority, a moral order in society and public conscience.
keyIdea: There must be no glaring inequalities and no oppressed class if democracy is to work.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 472–486

title: Filmed interview on the prospects of democracy in India
occasion: Short on-camera interview with a Western interviewer; dated 1953 by Frances Pritchett's timeline.
summary: A short filmed interview in which he talks about the prospects for democracy in India. It is not printed in BAWS.
keyIdea: A rare filmed record of him answering questions on Indian democracy.

source.label: Columbia University (Frances Pritchett) timeline, 1950s

audioOrVideo.note: Only copy found is a colourised upload by the YouTube channel "Buddhist Youth of India" (2020), credited "Black & White Video Courtesy: BBC Archive". No BBC-hosted original was found and the 1953 date rests only on Pritchett's timeline.

title: Osmania University Honoured Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
occasion: Special convocation conferring the honorary degree of Doctor of Literature (D.Litt.), 12 January 1953.
summary: Speech on receiving the honorary degree, recognising his work on the Constitution.
keyIdea: Recognition of the Constitution-maker by an Indian university.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 490–492

place: Rajya Sabha (Council of States), New Delhi
title: On the Andhra State Bill
occasion: Debate on creating Andhra State.
summary: Speaking about protecting minorities in multi-lingual states, he proposed special powers for governors and made his famous remarks that he had been "a hack" and would be "the first person to burn" the Constitution.
keyIdea: A constitution that does not protect minorities is not worth keeping.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 15, p. 851–864

place: Rajya Sabha (Council of States), New Delhi
title: On the International Situation (foreign policy)
occasion: Debate on foreign policy.
summary: He discussed the principles on which the government's foreign policy was based.
keyIdea: Foreign policy must rest on clear principles.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 15, p. 874–886

place: Rajya Sabha (Council of States), New Delhi
title: On the Report of the Commissioner for Scheduled Castes and Tribes for 1953
occasion: Debate on the annual report.
summary: He criticised the government's record on the welfare of Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
keyIdea: Constitutional safeguards mean little without real action.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 15, p. 895–918

place: Rajya Sabha (Council of States), New Delhi
title: On the Untouchability (Offences) Bill
occasion: Debate on the bill to punish the practice of untouchability.
summary: He spoke on how the law against untouchability should work in practice.
keyIdea: Laws against untouchability must be strong enough to be enforced.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 15, p. 925–943

title: My Philosophy of Life
occasion: Radio talk.
summary: He rejected the social philosophy of the Bhagavad Gita and said his own philosophy rested on liberty, equality and fraternity, which he had derived from the teachings of the Buddha and not from the French Revolution.
keyIdea: His philosophy had roots in religion, not in political science.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 503

title: Buddhist Movement in India: A Blue Print
occasion: Third conference of the World Fellowship of Buddhists.
summary: He set out a plan for spreading Buddhism in India, warning Buddhist organisations not to repeat the mistakes of Christian missionaries who first tried to convert the Brahmins.
keyIdea: Buddhism needs organised effort to revive in India.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 506–512

title: BBC radio interview
occasion: Interview recorded for the BBC; the interviewer is not named in the published version.
summary: In this 21-minute audio interview he discusses, among other things, his differences with Gandhi. It is not printed in BAWS.
keyIdea: His own account, in his own voice, of his disagreements with Gandhi.

source.label: BBC News India (official YouTube channel) – "Bhimrao Ambedkar's iconic interview from 1955 | Archives" (uploaded 17 March 2023)

audioOrVideo.note: BBC archive audio laid over archival footage, published by BBC News India (21:40). Frances Pritchett's 1950s timeline also links it.

place: Rajya Sabha (Council of States), New Delhi
title: On the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Bill
occasion: Debate on amending the right to property.
summary: Answering a taunt about his earlier remark on burning the Constitution, he explained it with the image of a temple taken over by a devil before the god could be installed.
keyIdea: A good constitution can be spoiled by those who work it.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 15, p. 944–961

place: Rajya Sabha (Council of States), New Delhi
title: On the States Reorganisation Bill
occasion: Debate on redrawing state boundaries.
summary: He said the storm centre of the debate was the position given to the City of Bombay, and discussed the problems of linguistic states.
keyIdea: States should be organised so that no community can dominate others.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 15, p. 962–973

title: Why I Like Buddhism
occasion: Talk for the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), London, dated 12 May 1956 (BAWS note), answering two questions: why he preferred Buddhism and how useful it was to the world.
summary: He said Buddhism alone combined three principles – prajna (understanding as against superstition), karuna (love) and samata (equality).
keyIdea: Understanding, love and equality together make Buddhism suited to the modern world.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 515–516

title: Prospects of Democracy in India
occasion: Broadcast talk for the Voice of America.
summary: He argued that India's caste system, which divided society into exclusive groups, was a standing denial of the ideals that democracy needs.
keyIdea: The caste system is a standing denial of democracy.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 519–523

title: The Tide of Buddhism Would Never Recede in India
occasion: Meeting for the 2500th Buddha Jayanti.
summary: After speaking on the life of the Buddha, he declared that he would embrace Buddhism in October 1956.
keyIdea: Buddhism, once revived, will not disappear from India again.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 517–518

title: Speech after the conversion to Buddhism (Diksha)
occasion: The day after the mass conversion ceremony of 14 October 1956; spoken in Marathi.
summary: He explained why the ceremony was held at Nagpur (land of the Naga people who spread Buddhism), why he chose Buddhism, and what the new Buddhists must do.
keyIdea: Conversion means a new life of equality and self-respect.

source.label: Columbia University (Frances Pritchett) – "Why Was Nagpur Chosen?", translated by Rekha Damle and Eleanor Zelliot from Prabuddh Bharat, 27 Oct 1956

title: Buddha or Karl Marx
occasion: Address at the end of the fourth conference of the World Fellowship of Buddhists (BAWS says it was delivered in the palace of the King of Nepal).
summary: He compared the Buddha and Marx and argued that the Buddha's non-violent way can achieve equality without dictatorship.
keyIdea: The Buddha's path achieves justice without violence.

source.label: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS) Vol. 17 Part 3, p. 549–559

audioOrVideo.note: A recording labelled as this speech was uploaded in 2021 by the YouTube channel "Buddhist Youth of India" without stating where the audio came from. Treat as unverified.
